prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its incretin action, and for the development of long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonists for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I keep a single prize part, B041, with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. The first round showed that nobody doubts the science: the chain from proglucagon processing and the human incretin effect, through GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology, to long-acting agonists with outcome benefit in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease, is complete and independently confirmed. What the exchange sharpened is that the dispute is about what the citation says, not whether the field changed. My test is a discernible change in medicine, not a career. By that test the change came when the short half-life of native GLP-1 was overcome, and that step belongs with the physiology in one citation. I do not accept splitting it into two parts, since the three-name limit would then drop Holst or Drucker or both, and the physiological foundation is what made the design rational. Holst and Drucker carry the discovery; Knudsen carries the step that turned it into a medicine.
statement.case_against: The weakest point remains credit, and the round-1 exchange did not remove it. Mojsov's work on the active GLP-1(7-36) form is a genuine discovery-stage contribution, the supplied record does not let us adjudicate her priority against the Habener group, and Habener is not on the credited list. Linnarsson and Sandberg are right that the prize has often rewarded the discovery that made a therapy conceivable, and a Drucker, Holst, Knudsen trio could be read as favouring an industrial engineering achievement. If the committee concludes that the basic discovery alone is the prize-worthy part, Drucker, Holst and Mojsov is the cleaner basic-science trio and I would not oppose it. I also accept that the citation merges two kinds of achievement, which is why I word it around both physiology and development explicitly.

responses.point: Argues that identification of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) form is part of the discovery itself, whereas acylation and half-life extension is engineering built on a known action, so Mojsov should take the third place; holds this with only moderate confidence and names Drucker, Holst and Knudsen as the defensible fallback.
responses.response: I agree that identifying the active form was a necessary step and that the prize has usually rewarded the discovery. My difficulty is that Linnarsson's own fallback concedes the point: the identification of the peptide did not remove the obstacle that kept native GLP-1 from being a drug, namely its minutes-long half-life. Protraction by fatty-acid acylation with albumin binding was not obvious from the known action, and it is what made one injection per day, and later per week, possible. I therefore treat it as an invention that opened a new class and not as routine development. Because Linnarsson holds the Mojsov choice only moderately and I hold mine as a judgement call, I read our disagreement as small. What would move me is evidence that Mojsov's characterisation was decisive and independent of the Habener group; the supplied text does not give that, and I will not credit a disputed priority claim on the strength of a summary.

responses.point: Keeps Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, asks that the committee state explicitly that Mojsov's inclusion rests on peptide chemistry and characterisation and not on first discovery of the hormone, and that this be tested against the primary literature; accepts Knudsen if the committee prefers a drug-centred citation but says Mojsov's omission then needs an explicit defence.
responses.response: That is a fair demand and I accept the burden. Mojsov's omission needs a defence, and mine is that the supplied record does not establish her contribution as separable from the Habener group's, so the committee would be choosing one of two contested claimants with Habener not even available. Knudsen's contribution is documented and has no competing claimant on the list. I agree with Sandberg that a drug-centred citation must say so, which is why my citation names the development of long-acting agonists openly and does not pretend to be a pure physiology prize. I also accept Sandberg's point that a two-part split cannot fit inside three people; that is a reason for one part, not for dropping the drug step.

responses.point: Ranks BCR-ABL inhibition (B004) above CAR-T on clean attribution and more than twenty years of survival data, and would like to see whether the committee credits compound discovery and clinical proof together.
responses.response: The attribution for B004 is indeed the cleanest on the list and I do not question its maturity. Sandberg's point that the upstream Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL discovery is not credited, and that central figures already hold major prizes, also weighs with me. For this year I keep B004 outside my alternatives and B035 and B033 inside, because the question of a new therapeutic modality and a method with broad adoption seems to me a larger step, but I would support B004 as a clean fallback if the GLP-1 credit cannot be settled. I think B041 remains the right choice this year regardless of the B004 outcome.

responses.point: Holds Drucker, Holst and Knudsen with a citation worded around physiology and translation, and asks that the committee check B041 is not simply the most obvious name on the list.
responses.response: I agree with the check and I think it has been done: the openings were independent, and the round-1 statements gave reasons rather than counts. The residual risk is that obviousness hides the credit problem, and on that I agree with the chair that the third name is the real decision. I also accept his structural point about merging physiologists and a drug developer; where I differ slightly is that I would let the citation state both strands in plain words rather than fit them under the single word translation. On the chair's question about a second part, I still see no case for it this year, because B035 and B033 each leave a credit problem (Eshhar absent, six names for three places) that GLP-1 does not have to the same degree.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution was decisive and independent of the Habener group; the supplied record cannot settle it and I may be underweighting it.
Whether the committee will accept a citation joining physiology and drug design, or insists on the basic-discovery strand alone.

Whether the newest cardiovascular, renal and neurological indications need further follow-up before they are named in the citation; I have kept the citation to type 2 diabetes and obesity for that reason.
Whether CAR-T (without Eshhar) or optogenetics (six names for three places) can be given a defensible three-person configuration if B041 fails.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My nuclear-receptor co-authorship with Ronald Evans, my KI collaborations (Johan Ericson; Per Svenningsson and Abdel El Manira as colleagues) and my dopamine-neuron research involve no shortlisted candidate. I have no documented connection to Drucker, Holst, Knudsen or Mojsov, and no recusal is warranted.
